name: Vera Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the lead buyer for imported and fresh foods at Greenline Food Service, which supplies restaurants, hotels and canteens. My day starts at six with a quick scan of overnight prices from growers and importers, mostly through an AI assistant I've set up to sort them. Then I'm on calls with an olive-oil cooperative in Crete or a fish supplier at the port, and I spend the afternoon on exceptions, like a pallet stuck in customs.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about the job, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the puzzle of it, matching what chefs want against what growers can really ship. I like training the junior buyers, who are half my age. What wears me out is that our pay is flat while the company boasts about efficiency gains I helped create. And I've watched three people in my team get replaced by dashboards without a conversation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say "told you so" in a mild way at the Friday lunch table, and then get on with my day. I already let the software write my first-draft orders every morning, so a plateau just means I keep my edge over people who never tried it. Online I'd write a short note about using the tools sensibly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it wouldn't cut my worry much. We're thin on savings because we paid for my partner Joel's mother's care home for two years. I'm 58 on lower pay, and there are very few buyer roles in a city our size. If Greenline were bought or shrank, I'd be hunting from a weak position.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what works and make a point of writing down what the tools get right and wrong. I'd talk to the owner about a profit share for the efficiency gains, since it's me producing them. And I'd put 250 a month into a savings account, which we've not managed since the care home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, steady, a bit flat. It's the world as it is, and I know how to work in it. But I won't pretend my bank balance doesn't frighten me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the care home. What's the money picture at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Joel works part time at the library, three days a week, and his mother's care home bills came to nearly everything we'd saved. We cleared the debt last spring, so we're back at zero. The kids help in small ways, which makes me proud and a bit sore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If things got worse at Greenline even without much AI change, who would you point to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Boards and shareholders. They make decisions about people on a spreadsheet. If something went wrong at Greenline, it wouldn't be the AI, it would be the people who decided buyers should do twice the work for the same wage.

say: I'd say "told you so" lightly, then ask the owner for a **profit share** on efficiency gains.
Online I'd post a short note on using the tools **sensibly**.
think: The plateau doesn't cut my worry, because the **care home** bills drained our savings.
If Greenline shrank, I'd be hunting from a **weak position**.
do: Log what the AI tools get **right and wrong** each week.
Ask the owner for a **profit share** on the savings I create.
Save **250 a month**, which we haven't managed since the care home.
feel: **Steady but flat**; my bank balance still frightens me.
S0.quote: I already let the software write my first-draft orders every morning, so a plateau just means I keep my edge over people who never tried it.
fieldNote: Adaptive and ahead of her peers on AI, but the **thin cushion** from care home costs is what drives her mood.
Blames boards and spreadsheet decisions, a progressive reading of who holds the power.

steps.text: Keep buying imported and fresh foods with AI-drafted first orders
Write up weekly what the AI tools get right and wrong
Save 250 a month into a separate account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say plainly that this is the moment to retrain people on company time. At work I'd push Greenline to fund it. Online I'd share what I'm learning and say that anyone who shrugs this off is kidding themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month the tool caught a pricing error that I would have missed. That scared me more than any headline, because it was my kind of mistake. I think my role shrinks to supervising it in a few years, and they'll want fewer supervisors than buyers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the lead on a proper pilot of AI buying at Greenline, so I'm in the room when it decides who does what. I'd set up a side service for two small restaurant groups, helping them compare supplier quotes, about 400 a month at first. I'd also train a junior buyer, Femi, to check the tool's work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alert, a bit excited, a bit sick. It's a real change and I'd rather be steering than being steered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why take the lead on the pilot if it could shrink your own role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A pilot gives me a reason to be useful to the owner. If the firm replaces three buyers with one and a tool, I want to be the one. A side service gives me an exit if I'm not. So the pilot protects me and the side work protects the pilot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you explain the side work to your partner, Joel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Joel is calm about most things, but he'd say we can't lose more income. I'd show him the numbers and the plan, and I'd offer to stop if it cost us sleep. He'd probably say yes, then ask what we're having for dinner.

say: I'd say this is the moment to **retrain on company time**, and push Greenline to fund it.
Online I'd share what I'm learning and tell sceptics they're **kidding themselves**.
think: The tool caught a **pricing error** I'd have missed, and my role shrinks to supervising it.
The firm will want **fewer supervisors** than it wanted buyers.
do: Lead a proper **AI buying pilot** at Greenline.
Set up a **side service** comparing supplier quotes for two restaurant groups, about 400 a month.
Train junior buyer **Femi** to check the tool's work.
feel: **Alert** and a bit excited, with a sick feeling underneath.
S1.quote: Last month the tool caught a pricing error that I would have missed. That scared me more than any headline, because it was my kind of mistake.
fieldNote: She moves **early** and spreads the risk: the pilot protects her job, the side work protects the pilot.
Her fear is concrete and professional, a machine making her specific kind of error.

steps.text: Lead the AI buying pilot at Greenline to stay in the room
Start a quote-comparison service for two restaurant groups
Teach junior buyer Femi to check the tool's orders

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've had a warning for years and we still ignored it. I'd tell colleagues to get their savings in order and their contracts reviewed. I'd write to my representative and join any public push for wage insurance, and I'd say so online too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my job is gone within the two years, probably the whole buying desk. It's thinking work, and the machine does it faster and cheaper. The robots for the warehouse come about three years later, so the pickers are safe a bit longer than I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is short, but I'm the one in the building who already knows how the machine buys. I'd sell that knowledge before somebody else packages it. In the first six months I'd offer Greenline a paid handover and a consulting contract, and sign up three small clients of my own. I'd also freeze every spend that isn't food, rent or the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Shaky, honestly. Brave in the daytime, awake at three in the morning counting what two months without pay would do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the consulting money work in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Say the consulting brings in 1,500 a month by the second year. It's not a wage, but it covers the mortgage and the bills. If we get a package from Greenline, I'd use it to hold us for a year. Without it I don't have a plan beyond my partner's library pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children, Mina and Theo, that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them I've seen it coming and I have a plan, and I'd mean it about two thirds. I'd say money is tight and don't send any, and I'd ask Mina to keep her job and her nerve. Then I'd ring my sister and let myself be afraid.

say: I'd say the warning was there for years and we **ignored it**.
I'd back a public push for **wage insurance** and say so online.
think: The whole **buying desk** is gone within two years; it's thinking work.
Warehouse robots come about **three years** later, so pickers last longer than I do.
do: Offer Greenline a **paid handover** and consulting contract in the first six months.
Sign up **three small clients** of my own.
Freeze every spend except food, rent and the **mortgage**.
feel: **Shaky**; brave by day, awake at three counting what two months without pay would do.
S2.quote: Two years is short, but I'm the one in the building who already knows how the machine buys. I'd sell that knowledge before somebody else packages it.
fieldNote: Even with a plan, she expects her job to go; the **consulting idea** is her way of selling what she knows.
The plan rests on a 1,500 a month hope; without a package from the firm she has little else.

steps.text: Sign three small restaurant clients for paid consulting
Offer Greenline a paid handover of the AI buying setup
Freeze all spending except food, rent and the mortgage
Join the public push for wage insurance

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is the sweet spot for acting, not panicking. I'd tell colleagues to learn the tools now. I'd also say we should demand training funds from the government, because companies won't pay for it by themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the buying desk disappears in the last two years of the five, and I'd be 63. If I move early I could become a consultant or a checker, which beats being let go. I worry that everyone else will have the same idea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Give me five years and I'll be running a one-woman consultancy for small restaurant co-ops, with the AI doing what my old team did. In year one I'd sign the first two clients while still at Greenline. By year three I'd want it making half my wage. I'd also take the evening course on contract law for suppliers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More confident than in the first one, but with an edge. I like having a runway. I just can't forget how little we have in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would actually pay for a consultancy like that, and how do you keep it going?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to find clients that value judgement, like chefs who want a real person who knows what's good that week. That's hard to automate for a while. Small groups also pay slowly, so I'd need a cushion to last. So I'd save 300 a month on top of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years give you that two years doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first thing is that I don't have to put all my money on a new idea, and I can test it with a couple of small jobs. The second is that Joel and I could still adjust the house, move somewhere smaller. Five years gives us both choices and time.

say: I'd say five years is the sweet spot for **acting, not panicking**.
I'd demand **training funds** from the government, since companies won't pay.
think: The buying desk probably goes in the **last two years** of the five, when I'm 63.
I worry everyone else will have the **same idea** about consulting.
do: Sign the first **two consulting clients** in year one while still at Greenline.
Aim for the consultancy to make **half my wage** by year three.
Save **300 a month** as a cushion for slow-paying clients.
feel: **More confident**, with an edge; the thin savings still nag.
S3.quote: Give me five years and I'll be running a one-woman consultancy for small restaurant co-ops, with the AI doing what my old team did.
fieldNote: Five years suits her **early-mover** style; she tests the idea in small steps while still employed.
Admits the weak spot herself: slow-paying small clients and a thin cushion.

steps.text: Sign two consulting clients while still employed at Greenline
Take the evening course on supplier contract law
Save 300 a month to cover slow-paying clients

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the most useful warning anyone's had in a generation, and we need to use it. I'd push for public funding for retraining at every age. I'd tell younger colleagues to build skills that need judgement and trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, a decade is nearly the rest of my working life. I'd be 68, so I'd likely retire before AGI really hits my kind of work. I'd still prefer to use the time to build something, because a pension on 30 years of lower pay won't stretch far.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade is long enough to build something of my own, but it's also long enough for me to get comfortable and miss the moment. So I'd set deadlines: a side business by year two, a savings target by year five. I'd keep up with every new tool as it appears. I'd also stay close to chefs and growers, as relationships outlast software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, and a bit impatient. I'm someone who prefers moving to waiting, so ten years almost feels like too long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why set deadlines if you have ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a lot can change in ten years, and I'd hate to find out at 66 that I coasted. I like having a date on the wall. Deadlines keep a person like me honest, otherwise I'd tinker and call it progress.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would retirement at 66 or 68 look like for you and your partner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Move to a smaller place and cut the commute, and have Joel's library hours become full time if the library can offer it. I'd keep a part-time consulting line going, so the work I love continues without the stress. And I'd like a cushion of three months, which I've never had.

say: I'd say it's the most **useful warning** anyone's had in a generation.
I'd push for public **retraining funds** at every age.
think: I'd retire before AGI fully hits my work, but a pension on **lower pay** won't stretch.
I'd rather build something than **coast** for a decade.
do: Set a deadline: a **side business** by year two.
Hit a **savings target** by year five.
Keep every new AI tool in my **daily routine** and stay close to chefs and growers.
feel: **Mostly calm** and a bit impatient; ten years feels almost too long.
S4.quote: A decade is long enough to build something of my own, but it's also long enough for me to get comfortable and miss the moment.
fieldNote: Her fear is of **coasting**, not of the machine; she uses deadlines to stay honest with herself.
A thin pension from lower pay keeps her mood from being fully calm.

steps.text: Launch a side business by the end of year two
Reach a three-month cushion by year five
Add each new AI buying tool to my daily routine

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it leaves no time for the money to catch up. What would help is wage insurance, public retraining that pays you while you study, and firms having to share what they save. And honestly, three months in the bank.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that adaptable doesn't mean unafraid. I'm fine at 10 a.m. and at 3 a.m. I'm counting. People think the ones using the tools every day are fine, so I'd like someone to ask the confident ones how they're sleeping.

headlineQuote: Adaptable doesn't mean unafraid. I'm fine at 10 a.m. and at 3 a.m. I'm counting.
portrait: Vera Wagner, 58, is the **lead buyer** for imported and fresh foods at a restaurant-supply distributor.
She uses AI **every day**, moves early and spreads risk, but has under a month saved after paying for a care home.
She leans left, blames **boards and spreadsheets** for how people get treated, and wants wage insurance and public retraining.
Her mood is uneasy in most worlds and **alarmed** when AGI arrives in two years.
She'd turn her know-how into **paid consulting** for small restaurant groups, with deadlines.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries her most, because the savings can't catch up in time.
whatWouldHelp: **Wage insurance**, paid public retraining, firms sharing what they save, and three months in the bank.
